newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel mourns, defies world on Jewish settlement.
newsitem.headline: Israel mourns, defies world on Jewish settlement.

text.p: Israel on Friday defied world criticism of its plans to build a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem as it mourned seven schoolgirls killed by a Jordanian soldier.
The Foreign Ministry rejected as "unilateral" and "useless" a U.N. General Assembly resolution on Thursday calling on Israel to stop the settlement plan.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed the building would go ahead, even as his aides said they were exploring the possibility of a visit to Israel by Jordan's King Hussein and a meeting between Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.

"If anyone thinks the murder of little girls will bring this people to its knees...or that we will relinquish our birthright, holy land and eternal capital, he does not know the strength that exists in each person standing here around me today and in the entire nation," Netanyahu said at a funeral for four of the girls late on Thursday night.

King Hussein expressed a desire to visit the families of the girls, aged 12 to 13, killed at a border site nicknamed "The Island of Peace" when a Jordanian soldier opened fire on them during a school trip.
Arafat said in remarks broadcast on Friday, in which he expressed sorrow at the killing, that he would be willing to meet Netanyahu.
"I have no objection. The most important thing (is) how to push forward the peace process," he told Israel Radio.
On Thursday his aide Marwan Kanafani said a meeting could occur if it dealt with the Israeli settlement plan and Israeli troop redeployment in the West Bank.

Until a telephone call between Arafat and Netanyahu after the shooting, there had been no contact between the leaders since Arafat last week angrily rejected as too small a planned Israeli redeployment in the West Bank.
Netanyahu spokesman Shai Bazak told Reuters on Friday that Israel was checking the possibility of an Arafat meeting and a visit by King Hussein but "nothing has been set".
The U.N. General Assembly, by a vote of 130 to two, with two abstentions, called on Israel on Thursday to abandon plans approved last month to build Jewish homes in Arab East Jerusalem.
The United States and Israel cast the only negative votes on the resolution, similar to one vetoed by the United States in the Security Council last Friday.

Arafat on Friday went ahead with preparations for a meeting he has called of U.S., European and Arab envoys in Gaza on Saturday that he said was needed to save the Middle East peace process from a crisis over Israel's settlement plans.
Washington has said it would send Edward Abington, the U.S. consul general in Jerusalem, to the meeting.
In Washington on Thursday, House of Representatives Republican leaders led by Speaker Newt Gingrich told President Bill Clinton that U.S. participation in the Gaza conference was a mistake.
They said that by agreeing to take part, Washington was sending a message that it was possible to drive a wedge between the United States and Israel, which is not invited to the conference.
Thursday's attack put pressure on the United States to broker a swift end to the crisis in Israeli-Arab relations over plans for the 6,500-home settlement.
Western officials said the shooting would temporarily take the diplomatic heat off Netanyahu, who would be able to point to Arab violence as the greatest threat to peacemaking.
King Hussein, who signed a peace treaty with Israel in 1994, said this week that Netanyahu's settlement policy was pushing the Middle East "towards an abyss of bloodshed".

In an interview published on Friday in Israel's Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper but given before the shooting, Arafat said PLO-Israeli relations were in the deepest crisis since their 1993 Oslo peace accords.

"This is not just 'another crisis,'" he said. "This is the most serious crisis since the Oslo process began, and it has far-reaching implications. You can say the process has stopped. The government of Israel has stopped it."
